fl-table.label: Lay the Table
fl-table.tool_text: In the full site, Gemma lays the table with a full Flourish recipe, built around everything you've told her.

fl-eggs.label: The eggs
fl-eggs.moment: From the farm down the lane. The hens are laying well this week.

fl-greens.label: The greens
fl-greens.moment: Kale and parsley, picked twenty minutes ago.

fl-range.label: The range
fl-range.moment: It's been lit since six. The big pan's always on it in the morning.

fl-dresser.label: The dresser
fl-dresser.moment: Lentils, chickpeas, oats and seeds. Keep these jars full and there's always a good meal in the house.

fl-trug.label: The trug
fl-trug.moment: Straight out of the beds. Knock the soil off, but don't wash them until you need them.

fl-herbs.label: The herbs
fl-herbs.ref: the herbs on the window ledge
fl-herbs.moment: Rosemary, thyme and mint. They like the sun on this ledge.

fl-phonograph.label: The phonograph
fl-phonograph.moment: Give the handle a few turns and it plays. Well, it will once I've found the records. Grieg in the mornings, I think.

fl-window.label: The sea
fl-window.moment: The same bay as the other kitchen, but this side gets the morning sun.

fl-back-door.label: The garden door
fl-back-door.closed: The kitchen garden's for another day. Breathe in, though. That's the rosemary.

atoms.title: Eggs baked on a pan of greens
atoms.body: Wilt a big handful of kale or spinach in a pan with a little oil and garlic. Make two hollows, crack an egg into each, put the lid on and give it three or four minutes. Toast on the side.

atoms.title: Oats with a spoon of seeds
atoms.body: Make your porridge or overnight oats the usual way, then stir in a spoonful of pumpkin seeds, sunflower seeds and ground flax. They add protein, fibre and good fats, and the bowl keeps you going for longer.

atoms.title: Red lentil and carrot soup
atoms.body: Soften an onion and two grated carrots, add a cup of red lentils, a spoon of cumin and a litre of stock. Simmer for twenty minutes, until the lentils fall apart. A squeeze of lemon at the end.

atoms.title: Roast beetroot and lentil salad
atoms.body: Roast wedges of beetroot until they're sweet and sticky, then toss them with cooked green lentils, rocket, crumbled feta and a mustardy dressing. It's even better the next day.

atoms.title: Whatever's-in-the-trug frittata
atoms.body: Soften whatever vegetables you have in an ovenproof pan. Pour over six beaten eggs with a little cheese, cook gently until the edges set, then finish it under the grill. Cold slices make tomorrow's lunch.

atoms.title: Smashed chickpeas on toast
atoms.body: Mash a drained tin of chickpeas with lemon, olive oil, a little garlic and salt. Pile it on toast with sliced tomato. Five minutes, and it'll carry you through to the afternoon.

atoms.title: A green smoothie that tastes nice
atoms.body: A handful of spinach, a banana, a spoon of peanut butter, a few oats and a glass of milk. Blend it. You won't taste the spinach, honestly.

atoms.title: A Sunday cook-up for the week
atoms.body: On Sunday, cook a pot of grains, a tray of roast vegetables and a few boiled eggs. Then all week, breakfast and lunch are just a matter of putting things together.

atoms.title: Why a bit of protein at breakfast helps
atoms.body: Protein and fibre take longer to digest than sugar and white bread, so a breakfast with eggs, yoghurt, nuts or seeds tends to keep you full for longer and helps you skip the mid-morning slump.

atoms.title: Why lots of colours on the plate
atoms.body: Different coloured vegetables bring different things: orange carrots have beta-carotene, dark greens have folate and vitamin K, beetroot has nitrates. A plate with a few colours covers more ground, with no counting.

atoms.title: Kale, the cottage-garden green
atoms.body: Cottage gardeners grew kale for centuries because it stands through frost and keeps cropping when little else will. A cold snap even makes the leaves a little sweeter.
